vignette: An infant is found on ultrasound and autopsy to have complete absence of a kidney. Histologic examination of the renal fossa reveals no primordial renal tissue or remnants from which the organ could have developed. The pathologist is asked to classify this defect according to standardized morphogenesis terminology.
question: Which term best describes an absent organ caused by absent primordial tissue?

options.text: Aplasia — an absent organ despite the presence of primordial tissue
Hypoplasia — incomplete organ development with primordial tissue present
Agenesis — an absent organ due to absent primordial tissue
Disruption — secondary breakdown of tissue with normal developmental potential
Deformation — extrinsic mechanical distortion during the fetal period

explanation_correct: Agenesis is defined as the absence of an organ due to absence of primordial tissue; no precursor tissue is present to form the structure. This distinguishes it from aplasia, in which primordial tissue is present but the organ fails to develop. The distinction depends on whether a primordial anlage can be identified on histologic examination.

explanation_incorrect.A: Aplasia is an absent organ despite the presence of primordial tissue (eg, renal aplasia with a rudimentary blastema), which is not the case here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hypoplasia denotes incomplete organ development with primordial tissue present and a smaller-than-normal organ, not complete absence.
explanation_incorrect.D: Disruption is the secondary breakdown of tissue that had normal developmental potential (eg, amniotic band syndrome), not a failure of the primordium to form.
explanation_incorrect.E: Deformation is an extrinsic mechanical distortion occurring during the fetal period (eg, congenital torticollis), not absence of an organ.

educationalObjective: Agenesis is absence of an organ because primordial tissue is absent, unlike aplasia where the primordium is present.

vignette: A newborn presents with a cleft lip and palate. The committing team reviews other categories of birth defects: an infant with amniotic band syndrome causing digit amputation, another with congenital torticollis from uterine positioning, and a fetus with multiple anomalies stemming from severe oligohydramnios. The cleft lip/palate is explained as an intrinsic defect arising during the embryonic period.
question: Which term best describes an intrinsic developmental defect such as cleft lip/palate that occurs during the embryonic period?

options.text: Deformation — extrinsic mechanical distortion during the fetal period
Disruption — secondary breakdown of tissue with normal developmental potential
Sequence — abnormalities resulting from a single primary embryologic event
Malformation — intrinsic developmental defect during the embryonic period
Field defect — disturbance of tissues in a contiguous physical space

explanation_correct: A malformation is an intrinsic developmental defect arising during the embryonic period, and cleft lip/palate is the classic example. The original developmental potential of the tissue is abnormal from the start, distinguishing it from disruption (breakdown of normal tissue) or deformation (extrinsic mechanical distortion during the fetal period).

explanation_incorrect.A: Deformation is an extrinsic mechanical distortion occurring during the fetal period, as in congenital torticollis, not an intrinsic embryonic defect.
explanation_incorrect.B: Disruption is the secondary breakdown of tissue that had normal developmental potential (eg, amniotic band syndrome), not an intrinsic defect.
explanation_incorrect.C: Sequence describes multiple abnormalities resulting from a single primary embryologic event (eg, oligohydramnios leading to Potter sequence), not the primary defect itself.
explanation_incorrect.E: A field defect is a disturbance of tissues that develop in a contiguous physical space (eg, holoprosencephaly), not a single intrinsic defect like cleft lip/palate.

educationalObjective: Malformations are intrinsic developmental defects of the embryonic period; cleft lip/palate is the classic example.

vignette: A fetus with bilateral renal agenesis has severe oligohydramnios. At delivery the infant has flattened facies, compressed limbs, and pulmonary hypoplasia. All of these abnormalities are thought to arise from the single primary event of markedly reduced amniotic fluid. The neonatologist explains this as a recognizable pattern.
question: Which term best describes multiple abnormalities that result from a single primary embryologic event?

options.text: Sequence — abnormalities resulting from a single primary embryologic event
Malformation — an intrinsic developmental defect during the embryonic period
Field defect — disturbance of tissues in a contiguous physical space
Disruption — secondary breakdown of normal tissue
Aplasia — an absent organ despite the presence of primordial tissue

explanation_correct: A sequence is a pattern of multiple abnormalities that all result from a single primary embryologic event. Oligohydramnios from any cause leads to Potter sequence, with pulmonary hypoplasia, flattened facies, and limb deformities. Identifying the primary event explains the seemingly unrelated downstream defects.

explanation_incorrect.B: A malformation is an intrinsic developmental defect during the embryonic period (eg, cleft lip/palate), not a cascade from one primary event.
explanation_incorrect.C: A field defect involves disturbance of tissues developing in a contiguous physical space (eg, holoprosencephaly), not a chain of secondary effects.
explanation_incorrect.D: Disruption is the secondary breakdown of tissue that had normal developmental potential (eg, amniotic band syndrome), not a sequence.
explanation_incorrect.E: Aplasia is an absent organ despite the presence of primordial tissue, which describes a single organ defect rather than a cascade.

educationalObjective: A sequence is a cascade of anomalies from one primary event; oligohydramnios producing Potter sequence is the classic example.

vignette: Prenatal imaging of a fetus shows a single common ventricle, fused thalami, and severe midline facial anomalies including cyclopia. The defect involves failure of normal division of tissues that develop within a contiguous physical space in the embryonic brain and face. The genetics team classifies the defect by morphogenesis type.
question: Which term best describes a disturbance of tissues that develop in a contiguous physical space, as in holoprosencephaly?

options.text: Sequence — abnormalities from a single primary embryologic event
Disruption — secondary breakdown of normal tissue
Deformation — extrinsic mechanical distortion during the fetal period
Agenesis — absent organ due to absent primordial tissue
Field defect — disturbance of tissues in a contiguous physical space

explanation_correct: A field defect is a disturbance involving multiple tissues that develop in a contiguous physical space, and holoprosencephaly is the classic example. A single localized insult to the developing forebrain and midline face produces the spectrum of brain and facial anomalies. This differs from a sequence, where defects arise secondarily from one primary event.

explanation_incorrect.A: A sequence is a cascade of defects from one primary event (eg, oligohydramnios to Potter sequence), not a spatially contiguous tissue disturbance.
explanation_incorrect.B: Disruption is the breakdown of tissue that initially developed normally (eg, amniotic band syndrome), not a field-wide developmental disturbance.
explanation_incorrect.C: Deformation is extrinsic mechanical distortion during the fetal period (eg, congenital torticollis), not a contiguous field defect.
explanation_incorrect.D: Agenesis is absence of an organ from absent primordial tissue and does not describe a spatially distributed field defect.

educationalObjective: Field defects affect contiguous developing tissues; holoprosencephaly is the classic example.

vignette: A 4-year-old boy has global developmental delay and microcephaly. He has a smooth philtrum, thin vermillion border, small palpebral fissures, and a flat nasal bridge. He also has a history of limb dislocation and a congenital heart defect. His mother acknowledges heavy alcohol use throughout pregnancy. The pediatrician notes that one mechanism involves impaired migration of neuronal and glial cells.
question: Which of the following diagnoses best explains this child's findings?

options.text: Neonatal abstinence syndrome
Fetal alcohol syndrome
Maternal diabetes effects
Congenital hypothyroidism
Thalidomide embryopathy

explanation_correct: Fetal alcohol syndrome is one of the leading preventable causes of intellectual disability in the US and results from maternal alcohol use during pregnancy. Findings include developmental delay, microcephaly, a smooth philtrum, thin vermillion border, small palpebral fissures, flat nasal bridge, limb dislocation, and heart defects; severe cases may include holoprosencephaly. One mechanism is impaired migration of neuronal and glial cells, and treatment is supportive care.

explanation_incorrect.A: Neonatal abstinence syndrome follows maternal opioid use and causes irritability, tremors, high-pitched cry, and GI disturbances, not this characteristic facial and neurodevelopmental pattern.
explanation_incorrect.C: Maternal diabetes causes macrosomia, caudal regression, and cardiac defects, not microcephaly with smooth philtrum and thin vermillion border.
explanation_incorrect.D: Congenital hypothyroidism causes intellectual disability and growth failure but not the characteristic facial stigmata and limb dislocation of fetal alcohol syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.E: Thalidomide embryopathy causes phocomelia and limb defects, not the microcephaly, smooth philtrum, and developmental delay described.

educationalObjective: Fetal alcohol syndrome is a leading preventable cause of intellectual disability with microcephaly, smooth philtrum, thin vermillion border, and small palpebral fissures.

vignette: A newborn whose mother has opioid use disorder develops irritability, a high-pitched cry, tremors, tachypnea, sneezing, and diarrhea. Feeding is difficult because of uncoordinated sucking reflexes, and the infant later has a seizure. The care team notes that universal screening for substance use is recommended for all pregnant patients.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management?

options.text: Fetal alcohol syndrome; supportive care only
Maternal diabetes effects; monitor blood glucose
Neonatal abstinence syndrome; treat with methadone, morphine, or buprenorphine
Congenital hypothyroidism; start levothyroxine
Neonatal sepsis; give broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation_correct: Neonatal abstinence syndrome is a CNS, ANS, and GI disorder caused by maternal substance use, most commonly opioids. Newborns present with uncoordinated sucking, irritability, high-pitched crying, tremors, tachypnea, sneezing, diarrhea, and possibly seizures. Opioid withdrawal is treated with methadone, morphine, or buprenorphine, and universal screening for substance use in pregnancy is recommended.

explanation_incorrect.A: Fetal alcohol syndrome presents with characteristic facial anomalies, microcephaly, and developmental delay rather than acute withdrawal signs in the newborn period.
explanation_incorrect.B: Infants of diabetic mothers may have hypoglycemia and macrosomia, but they do not display the irritability, tremors, and GI disturbances of opioid withdrawal.
explanation_incorrect.D: Congenital hypothyroidism presents with hypotonia, poor feeding, and prolonged jaundice, not the hyperirritability and high-pitched cry of withdrawal.
explanation_incorrect.E: Neonatal sepsis can cause temperature instability and poor feeding but not the classic withdrawal signs of sneezing, tremors, and diarrhea with a known maternal opioid history.

educationalObjective: Neonatal abstinence syndrome from maternal opioids causes irritability, tremors, high-pitched cry, and GI symptoms; treat with methadone, morphine, or buprenorphine.

vignette: A teratology researcher is counseling students about the timing of toxic exposures. She notes that an exposure before implantation tends to produce either no effect or death of the conceptus, an exposure during weeks 3 through 7 causes major structural anomalies, and a later exposure produces growth impairment and functional problems. She asks which principle best summarizes these observations.
question: Which of the following statements best summarizes the timing of teratogen susceptibility?

options.text: The fetal period is the window of greatest susceptibility to major structural malformations
Before implantation, teratogens produce dose-dependent graded malformations
Organogenesis occurs after week 8, when teratogens affect growth but not structure
Teratogens act mainly during organogenesis before week 8; before implantation the effect is all-or-none; after week 8 growth and function are affected
The embryonic period begins after week 8 and is when most structural defects arise

explanation_correct: Teratogens are most susceptible during organogenesis in the embryonic period, before week 8 of development. Before implantation, the effect is all-or-none—either the embryo is unharmed or it dies. After week 8, during the fetal period, exposures primarily affect growth and function rather than producing major structural malformations.

explanation_incorrect.A: The fetal period (after week 8) mainly affects growth and function; major structural malformations arise during organogenesis before week 8.
explanation_incorrect.B: Before implantation the effect is all-or-none, not a graded dose-dependent spectrum of malformations.
explanation_incorrect.C: Organogenesis occurs during the embryonic period before week 8, which is precisely when teratogens can produce structural defects.
explanation_incorrect.E: The embryonic period is before week 8, not after it; it is the window when most major structural defects arise.

educationalObjective: Teratogens are most teratogenic during organogenesis before week 8; preimplantation effects are all-or-none, and fetal-period effects involve growth and function.
